name: Lumbar support cushion / seat wedge

lead: Lumbar cushions fill the gap between the lower back and a chair. Seat wedges tilt the pelvis forward. Both are cheap add-ons aimed at sitting comfort and posture.
The literature is thin and concerns back pain, not appearance.

paras: The cushion supports the lumbar curve and the wedge changes pelvic angle. A small 2000 study looked at paraspinal muscle activity with and without a cushion.[1]
No adverse effects are documented in the sources consulted.

lead: A lumbar support cushion is a pad placed between the lower back and a chair backrest to support the inward curve of the lumbar spine. A seat wedge is a tapered cushion that tilts the pelvis forward. Both are sold as chair add-ons for sitting posture and back comfort.

Published research is sparse. A small military-aviation study examined a lumbar cushion for pilots with low back pain, and many patents for inflatable and contoured lumbar cushions exist. No trials were found that test these products for appearance outcomes.[1][2]

paras: Patent records show lumbar cushions in contoured, adjustable and portable inflatable forms, including a 1989 US patent for a rotationally contoured cushion and several inflatable designs filed from 2002 onward.[2][3]

A 2000 study from Serbia examined eight military helicopter pilots with low back pain during prolonged forced sitting. It compared sitting with and without a lumbar support cushion on separate days, measuring paraspinal muscle activity as a possible contributor to pain.[1] No studies found of seat wedges or lumbar cushions for posture appearance.
